clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive ataxia caused by biallelic SETX mutations affecting senataxin, a DNA/RNA helicase involved in transcription termination, resolution of R-loops and DNA damage repair.
Onset is typically in adolescence or early adulthood, later than in AOA1, with progressive cerebellar ataxia and an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
A raised serum alpha-fetoprotein is a hallmark of AOA2 and the key biochemical discriminator from AOA1.
Oculomotor apraxia is present in only about half of patients and is less consistent than in AOA1; strabismus and gaze-evoked nystagmus are also seen.
Additional features include head and limb tremor, dystonia, chorea, pes cavus and sometimes mildly raised creatine kinase or hypercholesterolaemia.
SETX is allelic with an autosomal dominant juvenile motor neuron disorder (ALS4), so the same gene can produce distinct phenotypes depending on the variant and inheritance pattern.
Unlike ataxia-telangiectasia there is no telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, radiosensitivity or marked cancer predisposition.
Cerebellar and vermian atrophy is the usual imaging finding.
reference.pathophysiology: AOA2 arises from loss-of-function variants in SETX, encoding senataxin, a large helicase that acts on both DNA and RNA. Senataxin promotes efficient transcription termination and resolves R-loops, the hybrid structures formed when nascent RNA re-anneals to template DNA, and it also participates in the response to oxidative DNA damage. When senataxin is deficient, unresolved R-loops and accumulating DNA lesions destabilise the genome of vulnerable post-mitotic neurons. The cerebellar Purkinje cells and the dorsal root ganglion neurons are preferentially affected, generating progressive cerebellar degeneration together with a dorsal root ganglionopathy and axonal sensorimotor neuropathy. The consistent elevation of alpha-fetoprotein, shared with several other DNA-repair ataxias, provides a reliable diagnostic marker although its mechanistic basis remains unclear.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal dominant juvenile motor neuron disease (allelic SETX / ALS4)
Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay
SYNE1-related ataxia and other recessive cerebellar ataxias
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies demonstrating an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy
Brain MRI assessing cerebellar and vermian atrophy
Creatine kinase, lipid profile and immunoglobulins
SETX sequencing or a recessive ataxia gene panel
Electromyography if motor neuron overlap is suspected
redFlags: Rapid progression or prominent lower motor neuron signs suggesting a motor-neuron-disease overlap
Rapidly worsening ambulation out of keeping with the usually slow course
reference.prognosis: AOA2 is slowly progressive, with most patients losing independent ambulation over one to two decades. Cognition and life expectancy are relatively preserved in the majority.
pitfalls: Interpreting a raised alpha-fetoprotein as pointing only to ataxia-telangiectasia or to hepatic pathology, rather than to a recessive DNA-repair ataxia.
Expecting oculomotor apraxia in every case, when its absence does not exclude AOA2.
Overlooking the allelic relationship with dominant motor neuron disease when lower motor neuron features emerge.
Confusing AOA2 with AOA1 when alpha-fetoprotein is not measured.
management: Supportive neurorehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy, plus mobility aids as independent ambulation is lost over time
Management of the axonal sensorimotor neuropathy with orthoses and foot care, and symptomatic treatment of tremor, dystonia and chorea
Monitoring and treatment of the associated hypercholesterolaemia
Podiatric and orthopaedic care for pes cavus
Multidisciplinary neurology follow-up to track progressive cerebellar and neuropathic disability
Genetic counselling and family testing for this autosomal recessive SETX disorder, noting the same gene can cause dominant ALS4 with distinct variants
